Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette:
Arjun's story begins on a humid summer night two years ago, in the apartment he shared with his girlfriend Meera. They had been arguing for weeks about money, about trust, about the future-ordinary fights that had slowly warped into something sharp and unpredictable. That night, the argument turned physical. He remembered her hand connecting with his cheek, then a shove that sent him into the wall. He did not hit back. He stood there, arms half-raised, as she struck him again and again, her body close enough that he could smell the salt of her sweat and the metallic tang of her anger. He did not run, did not fight-he simply waited for it to stop. When it did, he walked out the door and never went back. But the smell stayed.

Now, at twenty-nine, Arjun runs a small convenience store in a suburban strip mall. The work is steady and solitary, which suited him at first. But the world of customers and deliveries has become a landscape of ambush. A man with unwashed clothing steps up to the counter, and the sour odor of body sweat cuts through the stale air of the shop-Arjun's chest tightens, his palms grow damp, and the memory of that night crashes over him in full, uninvited color. He does not see Meera's face; instead, he feels the impact, the humiliation, the paralysis. Sometimes, when the smell is strong enough, he finds himself trembling with a rage so pure it frightens him. He has snapped at regulars, told them to leave, and then spent hours hating himself for it.

There are other triggers he cannot predict. A customer asks about his weekend, and the conversation drifts toward relationships. If anyone mentions conflict, arguments, even advice about moving on, Arjun feels his throat close. He has learned to steer conversations toward sports or weather, and if that fails, he claims a headache and retreats to the back room. The shop has become a place of constant scanning: every unfamiliar face, every lingering customer, every person who approaches too quickly seems charged with potential threat. He has started closing earlier than necessary, afraid of the half-hour after sunset when the lighting in the parking lot feels too dim, too exposed.

At home, Arjun lives with his current partner, Anika. She knows about the past relationship but not the details. He cannot bring himself to tell her-partly because talking about it would drag him back into the visceral shame of those moments, and partly because he is convinced she would see him as weak, as someone who let himself be hurt. Inaction guilt gnaws at him daily: I will never forgive myself for not doing more. He replays the scene, imagining a version of himself who fought back, who grabbed her wrists, who left the room before anything started. But he did none of that. He has come to believe something fundamental is broken in him-that he cannot rely on his own instincts, his own body, to keep him safe. And his body proves it every night: despite being in a safe home, with a partner who loves him, his heart races when he hears footsteps outside, he lies awake for hours checking the locks, and sometimes he feels a wash of raw terror or rage without any image attached-just the emotion, electric and senseless.

The consequences have crept in quietly. He avoids his own store during the busiest hours, sacrificing income. He has stopped seeing friends who knew Meera, skip outings where conversation might turn personal. Anika has begun to complain that he seems distant, irritable, that he flinches when she touches him unexpectedly. Last week, after a nightmare left him gasping, she asked him straight: "What happened to you?" He could not answer. That was when he finally called a therapist-not because he believed talking would help, but because he was exhausted, and because a part of him, buried under the shame, still wanted to believe he could one day feel safe again.
